analysis.one_liner: Shields companies that supply raw materials for medical implants from lawsuits by injured patients.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in June 1994, the bill was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it very hard to sue a company that merely supplies raw materials or parts used in medical implants — things like polymers and metals that end up in pacemakers or hip joints. Patients could only sue such a supplier if they proved the supplier shipped material that failed the manufacturer's specifications, and they would have to clear new procedural hurdles first, including sworn statements from specialists before filing. It would override state liability law on these points. The argument for it was that lawsuits were driving suppliers out of the implant market and threatening the supply of life-saving devices.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that sell raw materials and bulk components to implant makers — chemical, polymer, and metals suppliers — would gain near-immunity from suits by patients hurt by implants, keeping their exposure only to cases where they shipped off-specification material. Implant device makers would benefit too, from a more stable supply of materials, and they would keep their own full liability.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Implant materials suppliers and device makers

how_it_helps.text: No patient could sue a raw-material or component supplier at all unless the supplier was a registered device maker or the implant's seller, and the supplier could only be held liable if the patient proved by a preponderance of the evidence that the supplier delivered material that did not meet agreed or published specifications and that this caused the harm [S3].

A patient would have to name the implant manufacturer in the suit, file sworn affidavits from qualified specialists stating the supplier's material caused the harm before the case could proceed, and could face dismissal with no discovery allowed against the supplier until the court ruled [S3].
Patients who named a supplier and lost as frivolous would have to pay the supplier's attorney fees and costs, and courts could award these when the claim was found meritless [S3].

The bill's findings argued that suppliers, who make up a tiny share of their markets, were exiting the implant business because defending suits cost more than the sales were worth, and that this threatened the availability of life-saving and life-enhancing implants [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by implants. If a device failed because of a material in it, they could still sue the implant maker, but they could no longer sue the raw-material or component supplier in almost any circumstance — even if the material was inside their body — and they would face new upfront costs and expert-affidavit requirements to reach a supplier in the narrow cases left open. The federal rules would override whatever state liability law provided.

drawbacks.text: The bill closes a courtroom door for injured patients: if an implant maker could not be sued, had limited assets, or was hard to identify, the materials supplier might be the only party able to pay for the harm, and the bill would largely take that option away [S3].

The new requirements — naming the manufacturer, obtaining written determinations from qualified specialists before filing, and risking fee-shifting if a claim is found frivolous — would raise the cost of pursuing legitimate claims and could deter injured patients with valid but hard-to-document cases [S3].
The bill applies to all suits filed after enactment, including ones where the injury or the conduct causing it happened earlier, changing the rules for people already harmed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill targeted was real and documented in its own findings: suppliers with tiny implant-related sales faced litigation costs far larger than those sales, and some were refusing to sell materials for implants [S3]. But the remedy is one-sided — it grants suppliers broad immunity and stacks procedural hurdles in front of injured patients, while leaving the question of whether the industry would actually restore supplies to the suppliers themselves. An honest reading is that it traded a concrete loss of legal recourse for injured patients against an uncertain gain in device availability.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled action on it, and it expired when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Joseph Lieberman introduced the bill on June 20, 1994, for himself and Senator David Durenberger; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
The bill drew six cosponsors — five Republicans and one Democrat [S4].
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, injured patients kept the legal rights they had under state law, and materials suppliers stayed exposed to lawsuits rather than gaining the immunity the bill would have given them. Implant makers gained nothing either, though suppliers' refusal to sell materials for implants — the problem the bill described — was left unsolved.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 20, 1994 and took no further action — no markup or vote — before the Congress ended

against.name: Association of Trial Lawyers of America (plaintiffs' bar)
against.what_they_did: Opposed liability shields and federal preemption of state tort claims during the tort-reform debates of this era

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: a Democratic senator introduced it and five of the six cosponsors were Republicans, but the bill never advanced far enough for a partisan floor fight.

industries.industry: Raw material and component suppliers to implant makers (chemical, polymer, and metals companies)
industries.note: The bill would have given them near-immunity from suits by patients harmed by implants, keeping liability only for shipping material that failed agreed specifications. Suppliers argued this was necessary to keep them selling materials for implants at all, which the bill's findings said was threatening device availability — but the direct cost of the immunity falls on injured patients.

Device makers keep their own full liability but would benefit from a steadier supply of raw materials and parts, which the bill's findings said was drying up. They could also run the motions to dismiss suppliers from cases on a supplier's behalf.

The bill eliminates nearly all suits against materials suppliers, adds pre-filing specialist affidavits, and shifts fees for claims found frivolous — shrinking the cases this bar could bring on behalf of injured patients.
